repetition.avoid: Item: music-alt, from the bridge to the last chord (vamp, larry-doo, work-with, lift). Verdict: repeat. Kind: segment shape (how it ends), with its lighting. What it repeats: the show has already ended a song by dropping the lights for a quiet moment in which the host, alone and unsure, offers something small, is told in one flat line that it fits, and is then inside a full-band last hook whose person has changed to take him and the viewer in. Do not end by making room for the host, and do not turn the changed hook on him or on the lens. A turn: not open this episode.
repetition.why: Judged against 001-pilot, the only aired episode, with its song script and staging open. Four of the five things I was asked to look at are clear. GENRE: fresh. Doo-wop, swung, brushes, no kick, claps or shouts; it will not be heard as the stomp-clap anthem coming back, though both are major-key group cheer with a nonsense-syllable hook from Hy and Dee. STRUCTURAL JOKE: fresh. The aired song made its joke with a spoken catchphrase in stop bars after each sung wish; this one makes it with a pun (the week's phrase ends on the genre's own syllable) and a key change. No bot, no count, no stamp, no stop bar in the verses. MESSAGE: up to the bridge it is not the aired theme. The aired song was about longing for a place and finding you are already in it; this is about handing over something small. A CHANGED WORD IN THE LAST HOOK: the format chapter asks for it and the gate ruled it bones for the present song. I do not count it alone. It is now three songs running, which is a tic for the scorecard, and here, unlike in the present song, the change is again a change of person that takes the listener in. THE ENDING is the repeat, and the writer was right to flag it. Aired, beat for beat: lights down and a spot on the host; he sings alone, soft and unsure (a wish for a song made of mouths); a flat line tells him it exists and he is in it; the frame becomes the last vignette in the row of things built, with a pin on him; lights up, full band, the chorus back with its person and tense changed so that everyone is inside; then his button and a band member's last word. The alternative: bulbs down to one spot; the host sings alone, one unsure note; a flat line tells him it fits; his card joins the row of members' tiles at the same size; every bulb on, full band, the hook back with its person changed, sung at him and then at the lens; then his button and two band members' last word. One sentence describes both without naming their subjects: at the song's quiet point the host offers something small and doubtful, a flat reply folds him in, and the last chorus returns with its person changed and him inside it. That is the joke test for a repeat, and the ledger's device list has the lighting by name (lights down and a spotlight for a near-sincere moment, then the punch). The feeling is the aired one by another road: the writer's own header says the band makes his note the song's home note, which is a place to belong. The key change itself is new and good; what repeats is who it is done for and what the last hook is then turned into. Because the aired chorus is the thing the audience quoted back most, the last hook is the worst place for a second song to rhyme with the first, and a second song ending this way starts a formula. Weighed and not counted: (1) the lyric heads two captioned lines with 'someone built a', over a roll of things members made, each landing in a frame as it is sung, two of them this episode's own earlier segments. That is the nearest the draft comes to the aired verses and to the old phrase; the verb is plain here and not a punch, the format chapter asks for named specifics drawn as they are sung, and nothing answers the lines, so I leave it, but the final review should count the word across the episode. (2) The mug landing in the game on its sung word with ADDED BY DAVE: nothing was asked for, no time is given, no declaration is made, so it is not the old runner. (3) The band's two cards beside the members' tiles at the same size is the show placing itself among the makers; it is this song's own joke before the bridge and passes, and becomes part of the repeat only when the host's card joins. Turned is not available: the episode's one turned item is its close.

message: A viewer leaves with this: people here hand over whatever they have, a whole simulator posted under the words 'best i can do' or a photo of a mug that ends up inside it, and somebody always works with it, down to the host's one wrong note. Up to the bridge that is the week's and nobody else's (swap the stories and the hook is gone, because the phrase is the pun), so it is the message the owner asked for and it is worn lightly; the last third, where a group makes room for the one who thought he had nothing and then sings it at the lens, could close a song in any week and is the nearest the song comes to saying its moral aloud.
airWhy: As written I would air the present song, because the alternative's last third is blocked at the gate and its opening re-tells the segment before it; up to the bridge it is the funnier and much the more interesting song, with its jokes in spoken lines and on cards where the engine can land them, and with a different ending and some distance from the coffee segment it is the one I would air.
inside: The hook itself is a callback, since a different character takes a member's phrase somewhere new, but in the present order it plays as a repeat: the coffee button has already turned the phrase from 'i' to 'we' seconds before, and the song then re-tells that segment's fact from the same post card and brings back a mug beside the kettle, which a viewer will take for the mug just filled. Four members in two segments each is light for David and cee (a tile and a credit, none of their words) but leans too hard twice: Dave's post is performed by his puppet and then read again from its card back to back, and Samantha, who spoke in the previous aired episode and is already named three times in the opening segment, is credited again. The song also brings no new person into the episode, and it would be a third segment that turns on the host's smallness and a third to end on him alone and dry about himself, after the account bit and the making-of.
